summary:
Consensual sexual conduct between adults is lawful in Saint Kitts and Nevis. On 29 August 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck sections 56 (buggery) and 57 (indecent assault against men) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy and freedom of expression. The decision took immediate effect and decriminalised consensual sexual intercourse between adult men in private, and the conduct has been legal throughout the country, on both Saint Kitts and Nevis, since that judgment. The offences struck were defined in relation to men, and the change came from a civil-society constitutional challenge rather than from legislation.

The penal code contains no protection against discrimination or harassment on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no post-repeal discrimination statute has been enacted. Discrimination in employment, education and accommodation, and hate speech, remain lawful. A visitor subjected to any of these has no local statutory remedy.

No form of same-sex union is recognised, whether marriage or partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the rights attaching to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as same-sex can expect no spousal recognition, no next-of-kin standing and no partner benefits under local law.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: there is no procedure for changing gender markers, and identity documents cannot be updated to reflect a trans person's gender. A trans visitor travels on the documents issued by their home jurisdiction and cannot have them altered locally.

Protection machinery is thin. The National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 names LGBTQ+ citizens among the groups it covers, but the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE told the Universal Periodic Review process in 2025 that the state has taken no tangible steps under it, and that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement. That avoidance is a direct signal about reporting: police are not a reliable route to protection for anti-trans harassment or assault. LGBTI organisations are permitted to register.

State posture toward LGBTQ people has been documented at the point of entry. On 23 March 2005 Nevis barred a cruise ship carrying 110 passengers, most of them LGBTQ, from docking; a police boat halted the Source Events/Windjammer Barefoot Cruises vessel and the ship was ordered to sail on. Port officials announced the exclusion publicly as a cultural decision, and the port authority's acting general manager, Oral Brandy, told reporters that Nevis did not want homosexuality "to be a part of our culture."

In 2011 the Government of Saint Kitts and Nevis stated that it had "no mandate from the people" to abolish the criminalisation of homosexuality among consenting adults, a position taken while the struck offences were still in force.
tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation rests on a court judgment rather than a parliamentary act. Human Dignity Trust documents a series of Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy laws, of which Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General is one, and 76 Crimes follows the same regional pattern of litigation-driven repeal. No successor statute addressing discrimination accompanied the judgment.

The ruling on the offences had regional reach: the same court decided challenges affecting neighbouring Eastern Caribbean states, which means the legal position in Saint Kitts and Nevis can shift with regional litigation rather than with domestic political change.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot change their legal gender. No gender identity recognition procedure exists, and identity documents cannot be updated to reflect a trans person's gender.

No form of relationship recognition is available to same-sex couples, neither marriage nor partnership, and same-sex households receive none of the rights held by opposite-sex married couples.

Discrimination protections are absent in employment, education and accommodation, and hate speech is not unlawful. The penal code does not address discrimination or harassment on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

LGBTQ+ organisations may register and operate. The Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE report that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, and that LGBTQ+ citizens are named in the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 but that the state has taken no tangible steps under it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prosecution, police and court practice toward trans or gender-nonconforming people after the 2022 judgment is not documented in the sources, and the frequency with which the struck provisions were applied before it is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence or hate-crime data for Saint Kitts and Nevis appears in the sources, and no comparison with the jurisdiction's general homicide rate is available.

Immigration and visa screening rules that would single out trans travellers are not sourced. The one documented exclusion at a port, the 2005 refusal of a chartered cruise ship, was an ad hoc decision by port authorities rather than a published entry rule.

Implementation of the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 rests on civil-society reporting to the Universal Periodic Review; no government implementation report was located. Country coverage in several sources comes from regional campaign and tag archives rather than country-specific enforcement reporting, so enforcement detail is unresolved.
